routes.description: Establish a historically credible body of postmortem-appearance data, defend supernatural events as admissible historical conclusions, and show that resurrection explains the relevant data better than the principal naturalistic alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the appearance traditions are sufficiently established, resurrection has greater comparative explanatory adequacy than rival accounts, and neither methodological naturalism nor uncertainty about the precise divine agent blocks the supernatural conclusion.

motionBridge.description: The historical evidence and relevant background information must make Jesus's resurrection the best explanation of the reported postmortem appearances.

centralBridges.description: Early and corroborated sources must establish individual, hostile, and group appearance claims as data requiring explanation.
Resurrection must provide greater explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and economy than hallucination or other naturalistic alternatives.
Historical inquiry must be able to recognize an event transcending known natural capacities without first identifying its precise supernatural agent.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Independent allegedly paranormal phenomena may supply background plausibility for admitting supernatural explanations.
Reliable ordinary testimonial evidence must be capable in principle of supporting an extraordinary historical event.

routes.description: Maintain that resurrection proponents bear the evidential burden, challenge the accessibility and reliability of the ancient appearance reports, and deny that unexplained events or defeated natural alternatives establish supernatural causation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the historical data remain insufficiently confirmed or if resurrection and divine agency cannot be warranted from those data, making suspension of belief appropriate without requiring proof that resurrection was impossible.

motionBridge.description: Belief in Jesus's resurrection must be withheld unless the affirmative evidence establishes both the alleged event and the inferential move to resurrection.

centralBridges.description: Ancient appearance reports must provide accessible, independently supportable evidence adequate to establish the claimed postmortem events.
An unexplained or anomalous event must not be treated as evidence of supernatural causation without a method that distinguishes that cause from error, fraud, hallucination, or unknown natural causes.
The resurrection hypothesis must supply testable or discriminating explanatory content rather than merely relabeling the absence of a natural explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The evidential limits created by two millennia of investigative distance must constrain comparisons with directly observable modern anomalies.
Attributing resurrection to divine action requires independent grounds for a capable and willing agent or evidence that itself discriminates in favor of such an agent.

sections.title: Historical foundation for the appearance claims
sections.rationale: The existence, independence, accessibility, and reliability of the Pauline, apostolic, individual, and group appearance traditions determine what historical data the competing explanations must address.

sections.title: Resurrection versus naturalistic explanations
sections.rationale: The motion turns centrally on whether resurrection explains the asserted historical data better than hallucination, error, dishonesty, or other naturalistic possibilities under comparative explanatory criteria.

sections.title: From anomaly to supernatural causation
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether an event judged incompatible with known natural capacities may be classified as supernatural or whether that classification merely substitutes a label for unresolved causation.

sections.title: Historical method and standards for extraordinary claims
sections.rationale: The parties' competing standards for testimony, repeatability, methodological naturalism, and investigation determine what kinds of evidence can justify an extraordinary historical conclusion.

sections.title: Background supernaturalism and identification of divine agency
sections.rationale: Allegedly paranormal phenomena and the question of prior grounds for God affect the background plausibility of resurrection and the further inference from a postmortem event to purposeful divine action.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-01.proposition: Multiple classes of allegedly paranormal experience collectively provide empirical support for a supernatural dimension of reality.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-02.proposition: Early Pauline material and apostolic corroboration support a historical bedrock of individual, hostile, and group resurrection-appearance experiences.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-03.proposition: Under explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and avoidance of ad hoc assumptions, resurrection explains the asserted historical bedrock better than hallucination.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-02.proposition: Scientific and historical disciplines use different investigative methods, so lack of controlled repeatability does not by itself disqualify supernatural claims from investigation.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-03.proposition: Methodological naturalism can exclude supernatural explanations in advance and prevent recognition of events that known natural causes cannot plausibly explain.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-04.proposition: Case-by-case comparison of hypotheses using the historical data and relevant background information favors resurrection over the proposed naturalistic alternatives.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-04.proposition: An extraordinary event does not require a special category of extraordinary evidence when sufficiently good ordinary eyewitness evidence supports it.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-06.proposition: A verified event impossible under known natural laws may be classified as supernatural even when its particular causal agent remains unidentified.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-08.proposition: Evidence for resurrection can itself support supernaturalism and probably theism without requiring a prior proof of God's existence.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-04.proposition: Belief in resurrection should be withheld unless its proponents discharge their evidential burden and show that the skeptical default is false.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-05.proposition: Reports of unexplained experiences do not establish a supernatural realm when that category remains poorly defined, unconfirmed, and causally uninvestigated.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-06.proposition: Eliminating a hoax or lacking a natural explanation does not establish resurrection, because attributing the event to divine action supplies no mechanism or explanatory content.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-07.proposition: Treating resurrection as plausible presupposes independent grounds for a God capable of and willing to raise Jesus, while private revelation is unverifiable hearsay to outsiders.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-08.proposition: Neither historical inquiry nor science can confirm supernatural causation without a workable account of what the supernatural is and how it causally operates.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-05.proposition: Methodological naturalism permits investigation of extraordinary events but withholds supernatural attribution until a testable model distinguishes genuine phenomena from fraud, error, and hallucination.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-07.proposition: Paul is a weak foundation for resurrection because he lacked direct access to Jesus's ministry, death, burial, and empty tomb, while surviving reports do not independently demonstrate a return from death.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-10.proposition: Calling an event supernatural merely labels the absence of a natural explanation and cannot justify specific conclusions about gods, spirits, souls, or resurrection.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-03.proposition: The claim that Jesus appeared to five hundred people lacks accessible identities, statements, and experiences sufficient to investigate whether the reported event occurred.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-05.proposition: Even observing an extraordinary return from death would justify accepting that the event occurred without justifying an unsupported supernatural causal explanation.
